title: Searching and hashing
kicker: ENCT 252 · Data Structure and Algorithms · Chapter 8
subtitle: From scanning every item to jumping straight to it — and what to do when two keys want the same slot.

sections.title: Sequential and binary search
sections.body: Sequential search checks items one by one: O(n), works on anything. Binary search needs sorted data: compare with the middle item, discard half, repeat — O(log n). One million sorted items need at most 20 probes.

worked.why: Worst case probes for n items is ⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Discarding half is only valid if order tells you which half.

figures.caption: Figure 8.1.1 — Sequential and binary search
figures.note: Probes 12, then 23, then 16: three steps for seven items.

sections.title: Hash tables
sections.body: A hash function turns a key into an array index, e.g. h(k) = k mod m. Lookup, insert and delete are O(1) on average. The table has m slots; the load factor α = n/m measures how full it is. A good hash spreads keys evenly; using a prime m helps.

choices.text: n / m — stored items divided by table slots.
The size of the hash function.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: As α rises, collisions become more likely.

sections.title: Collisions: chaining and open addressing
sections.body: Two keys with the same hash collide. Chaining: each slot holds a list; colliding keys join it. Open addressing: probe other slots in a fixed sequence until a free one is found — linear (h, h+1, h+2…), quadratic (h, h+1², h+2²…, avoids long runs), double hashing (step from a second hash). Insert 50 700 76 85 92 73 101 into 7 slots with linear probing: table 700 50 85 92 73 101 76.

questions.prompt: What problem does linear probing suffer from?

choices.text: Primary clustering: long runs of filled slots grow, making probes longer.
It needs a list per slot.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Keys landing in a run all extend it.

figures.caption: Figure 8.3.1 — linear probing
figures.note: Red slots were probed and found occupied.

figures.caption: Figure 8.3.2 — chaining
figures.note: Chaining keeps colliding keys in a list.

problems.prompt: Insert 50, 700, 76, 85, 92, 73, 101 into a table of size 7 with h(k) = k mod 7 and linear probing. Show the table.

sections.title: Cost of hashing
sections.body: With chaining the expected cost of an unsuccessful search is 1 + α probes. For open addressing with linear probing it is about ½(1 + 1/(1−α)²): it explodes as α → 1, so keep α below about 0.7 and resize (rehash into a bigger table) when it is exceeded.

questions.prompt: Why resize a hash table when it gets too full?

choices.text: Probe sequences and chains lengthen sharply, destroying O(1) behaviour.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Doubling and rehashing restores a low load factor.

sections.title: Where hashing is used
sections.body: Dictionaries and sets (C++ unordered_map), symbol tables in compilers, caches, database hash indexes, password storage (with a cryptographic hash) and file deduplication. Hash tables do not keep keys in order and have no fast range queries — a balanced tree or B-tree is better there.

sections.title: Summary
sections.body:
• Sequential O(n); binary O(log n) on sorted data; hashing O(1) average.
  • Collisions: chaining or probing; keep load factor low.
